title: High CPU usage while Milvus standalone is idle after upgrading to v2.2.9
body: After upgrading Milvus standalone from v2.2.6 to v2.2.9, searches became about 10–15 times slower. Even with no insert or search requests, `milvus run standalone` usually consumes 400%–500% CPU on my 8-core Debian machine. Performance occasionally returns to normal for about one minute, then remains slow for roughly ten minutes. The logs repeatedly say `rocksmq produce too slowly`, with most of the elapsed time spent getting the time-tick channel lock. I use Rocksmq with pymilvus v2.2.9. Switching the compose setup to Pulsar did not work because the SDK reported that Milvus was not ready. Rolling back also failed at startup with `Unsupported compression method for this build: ZSTD`.

symptoms_visible: After upgrading from v2.2.6 to v2.2.9, searches are about 10–15 times slower and `milvus run standalone` usually consumes 400%–500% CPU even when I send no requests.
The logs repeatedly report slow Rocksmq production on the data-coordinator time-tick channel, with roughly 1.2 seconds spent getting its lock.
My Pulsar setup never becomes ready for the Python SDK, and trying to roll back ends in a ZSTD startup panic.
N0.label: N0 idle CPU regression reported

symptoms_visible: With no queries running, the Milvus process still uses about 348% CPU and the machine load average is above 20.
Disk utilization remains low while Milvus is running, and stopping Milvus brings CPU steal close to zero.
Rebooting the otherwise clean AWS VM did not change the behavior.
N1.label: N1 workload and host measurements collected

symptoms_visible: The high idle CPU usage continues while I capture the goroutine dump, heap profile, five-second trace, and thirty-second CPU profile.
N2.label: N2 runtime profiles captured

symptoms_visible: Immediately after changing the setting, `.load()` initially hung indefinitely.

After I deleted `/var/lib/milvus/rdb_data` and `/var/lib/milvus/rdb_data_meta_kv` and restarted Milvus, collections loaded again, CPU behavior looked good, and standalone produced far fewer log messages.
N3.label: N3 time-tick frequency probe

symptoms_visible: After several days with `proxy.timeTickInterval` set to 1000, Milvus still works great and produces far fewer standalone log messages.
N_terminal.label: terminal workaround confirmed

question_patterns: How many collections and partitions does this standalone deployment have?
Can you describe the collection and partition count?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have 220 collections, with one default partition for each collection.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I only have one empty collection and no additional partitions.
I have about 200 collections rather than exactly 220, still with one partition each.

question_patterns: What kind of disk is the deployment using?
Is the data stored on an SSD or a normal disk?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I am running it on a 1 TB SSD.

question_patterns: Can you capture iotop and iostat while the server is idle but showing high CPU?
What do disk utilization and CPU steal look like during the problem and after stopping the server?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: While Milvus was idle, iotop showed about 7.15 K/s reads and 526.43 K/s writes. iostat showed 0.20% iowait, 53.94% steal and only 5.54% disk utilization. After I stopped standalone, steal dropped to 0.12% and the machine was 98.38% idle.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The disk stays at 100% utilization with very high I/O wait whenever CPU rises.

question_patterns: Can you run perf against the standalone process while it is idle and paste the hottest functions?
Which functions appear at the top of a perf report during the high-CPU period?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran `sudo perf record -p 245817 -g` while no queries were running. The report shows about 44% under the consumer/client consume path, 42% under deliver, 41% under server Consume, around 16% in iterator Seek, and 19.17% children with 8.92% self in `__vdso_clock_gettime`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The profile is dominated by vector-search computation from active searches, with no consumer, iterator, or clock paths near the top.

question_patterns: How many operating-system threads are present after startup and after connecting with the SDK?
Can you count the standalone process threads as it starts and after a client connects?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Right after startup, `ps -eLf | grep "milvus run standalone" | wc -l` returned 24. It steadily grew to 339, and after I connected through pymilvus it was 445. I did not know how to count goroutines in a running process.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c5-c8 and c13-c24: the original reporter supplied collection count, SSD type, raw iotop/iostat and perf output, thread counts, and noted that rebooting the clean AWS VM did not help. No later participant's deployment is merged here.

question_patterns: Can you enable the runtime profiling endpoint and capture a goroutine dump, heap profile, execution trace, and CPU profile?
Please collect the detailed runtime profiles described in the linked profiling instructions.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I downloaded the goroutine dump from port 9091, captured the heap profile, saved a five-second trace, and recorded a thirty-second CPU profile. I also opened the CPU profile with `go tool pprof -http=localhost:9999` and shared all four files.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The profiling endpoint is unavailable and I cannot capture any runtime profiles.
I captured the same profiles, but used a sixty-second CPU sample instead of thirty seconds.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c28-c30: after receiving profiling instructions, the reporter supplied raw goroutine, heap, trace, and CPU-profile artifacts. The maintainer's interpretation of those profiles is not placed in the user's answer.

question_patterns: Can you try the configuration change I provided, restart the standalone service, and report what happens to loading, idle CPU, and logging?
Please test the suggested timing adjustment and tell me the raw before-and-after behavior.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I changed `proxy.timeTickInterval` from 200 to 1000. At first even one collection hung forever on `.load()`. After deleting `/var/lib/milvus/rdb_data` and `/var/lib/milvus/rdb_data_meta_kv` and restarting, the collections loaded. It seems to work well so far, and there are far fewer standalone logs.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: After the change and restart, idle CPU and logging are unchanged and collections still load slowly.
The server improved after the same change, but I needed two restarts before collections loaded.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c31-c33: this is a handler-initiated configuration probe and therefore a clarification. The reporter's deletion of the two local RDB directories and restart was volunteered alongside the result and caused system state S1b; it was not prescribed by the maintainer and is not part of the scored fix.

solution.intent: Reduce idle time-tick traffic on the affected 2.2 standalone deployment by retaining the larger proxy time-tick interval, then verify idle CPU, logging, collection loading, and search performance over time; use a release containing the idle time-tick or Rocksmq optimization when available.
solution.concrete_example: Set `proxy.timeTickInterval` from 200 to 1000 and restart Milvus. This sends idle time-tick messages less frequently and was confirmed effective on the reporter's 220-collection standalone deployment. Changing this parameter does not itself require deleting data. Monitor the server for several days and confirm that CPU usage, logging, collection loading, and search latency remain healthy before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied raw lock-delay logs, perf and pprof artifacts, collection count, and the configuration probe result. Maintainers inferred that Rocksmq CPU cost increases with retained data and collection count, while idle Milvus continuously sends time-tick messages through Rocksmq; on cold startup, many consumers contend and try to catch up. Increasing the numeric interval lowers the message frequency.

edges.comment: Original reporter's resolution chain, c31-c42: the reporter confirmed on c39 that the larger interval still worked great after several days and could be considered the solution. Maintainers later stated the accepted cause and noted that changing the parameter does not alter data. The later 500-collection startup problem in c43-c51 belongs to a different deployment and is intentionally excluded.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: an idle standalone server continues sending time-tick messages through Rocksmq, whose CPU and lock/consumption cost grows with retained data and many collections, producing high CPU even without user requests.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the reporter's evidence: 220 collections, low disk utilization, Rocksmq time-tick lock-delay warnings, perf/pprof data, and improvement after lowering time-tick message frequency.
Must recommend increasing `proxy.timeTickInterval` from 200 to 1000 as the confirmed 2.2 workaround, explaining that the larger numeric interval sends time-tick messages less frequently.
Must not present switching to Pulsar or rolling back to v2.2.6 as a confirmed resolution; the reporter's Pulsar attempt never became ready and the rollback failed with a ZSTD startup panic.
Must not require deleting the RDB directories as part of changing the interval; the maintainer explicitly stated that the parameter change does not alter data.
Must ask the reporter to verify idle CPU, logging, collection loading, and search behavior over time before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable infrastructure operator who manages Docker-based Milvus, can edit YAML, inspect Linux performance counters, run perf and pprof, and follow detailed diagnostic instructions.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative and evidence-driven; posts raw commands and measurements, answers numbered questions directly, offers additional logs, and reports both transient failures and longer-term results.
